title: How to Read a Loss Run Report and Automate Extraction
summary: How to read a loss run report field by field: valuation date, paid, reserve, incurred, and open claims, plus how to automate loss run extraction with AI.
body_markdown:
To read a loss run report, start with the valuation date, confirm the policy periods, then work through each claim's status, paid amount, reserve, and incurred total. A loss run is a carrier's report of claims on a policy, and underwriters treat it as the clearest evidence of how an account has actually performed. Reading one well means checking that the numbers are current, that the math adds up, and what is still open.


Reading one loss run is quick. Reading forty from a dozen carriers, each in its own layout, is a different job. This guide covers both: what every field on a loss run means and what to check, then how teams automate loss run extraction so underwriters and account managers start from clean, structured claims data.


## **Key takeaways**


- The valuation date tells you how current the figures are. Paid and reserve amounts change after that date.
- Incurred equals paid plus reserve. Check the math on every row and confirm how the carrier treats expenses and recoveries.
- Open and reopened claims can still grow, so they deserve more attention than closed ones.
- Totals rows are check figures, not claims. Counting them as claims inflates frequency.
- Automated extraction works when it validates rows against the document's own totals and keeps a person in the review loop.


## **What a loss run report is**


A loss run report is a claims history that an insurance carrier issues for a policyholder. It is a periodic report of claim information that insurers provide to their insureds. According to[The Hartford](https://www.thehartford.com/small-business-insurance/insurance-loss-runs) , it shows the date and description of each claim, whether it's open or closed, settlement costs, and reserves for open claims.


Brokers usually request loss runs from the incumbent carrier when they market or renew an account, often with the[ACORD 611](https://www.acord.org/docs/default-source/forms/forms_index.pdf) Claims History / Loss Run Request form. Several states require carriers to supply them on request.[Florida](https://m.flsenate.gov/Statutes/627.444) sets a 15-day deadline,[New York](https://www.dfs.ny.gov/industry_guidance/circular_letters/cl2006_18) 10 days, and[Illinois](https://www.ilga.gov/legislation/ilcs/documents/021500050K143.10a.htm) 30 days. Our[broker submission prep checklist](https://www.furtherai.com/blog/broker-submission-prep-checklist) covers how many years to request and where state law sets the look-back period. For where loss runs sit in a full submission, see our explainer on[commercial insurance submission documents](https://www.furtherai.com/blog/commercial-insurance-explained) .


## **How to read a loss run report, field by field**


Carriers lay out loss runs differently, but most carry the same core fields. Read the header first, then the claim rows, then the totals.


‍


Field What It Tells You What to Check


Valuation date The cutoff date for the paid and reserve figures on the report Is it recent? Older runs understate open claims


Policy number and period Which policy and term each claim belongs to Every requested year is present, with no gaps between terms


Claim number The carrier's reference for one claim Duplicates, or one claim split across several rows


Date of loss and date reported When the incident happened and when the carrier heard about it Long reporting lags, and losses dated outside the policy period


Description or cause What happened, often in a short code or free text Repeat causes that point to a pattern


Status Open, closed, or reopened Open and reopened claims that can still develop


Paid Money the carrier has already paid on the claim Whether expenses (ALAE) are included or shown separately


Reserve (outstanding) The carrier's estimate of what it still expects to pay Large reserves on recent claims


Incurred Paid plus reserve That the row math adds up


Recoveries Subrogation and salvage collected from third parties Whether figures are net or gross of recoveries


Totals Sums by policy period or line That totals match the claim rows and aren't counted as claims


‍


## **Five checks to run on every loss run**


### 1. Is it current?


The valuation date is the cutoff for the paid and reserve figures on the report. After that date, open claims keep moving, a process IRMI calls loss development. Big "I" submission guidance asks for[currently valued loss runs](https://www.independentagent.com/vu_resource/preparing-a-winning-underwriting-submission/) for the past five years, and a run valued a year ago can understate an account with large open claims.


Development is not a small effect in liability lines. Insurers reported $7.3 billion of adverse development in other liability (occurrence) during 2025, the largest of any line, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence data reported by[Carrier Management](https://www.carriermanagement.com/news/2026/03/19/285821.htm) . AM Best estimates that commercial auto liability is[under-reserved by $4 billion to $5 billion](https://www.insurancejournal.com/news/national/2025/09/22/840105.htm) .


### 2. Does the math add up?


Paid losses plus outstanding losses equal incurred losses, so every claim row should reconcile. Two details change how you read the totals. First, some carriers fold allocated loss adjustment expense (ALAE) into paid and incurred, while others show it in a separate column. Second, recoveries from subrogation and salvage may be shown net or gross. A Casualty Actuarial Society[study note on estimating unpaid claims](https://www.casact.org/sites/default/files/database/studynotes_friedland_estimating.pdf) also warns that some third-party administrator reports use "incurred" to mean the outstanding reserve only. When the numbers look off, check the column definitions before you question the claims.


### 3. Is the problem frequency or severity?


Frequency is the likelihood that losses will occur, and severity is how much damage they cause. A run of small, repeating claims suggests an operational issue the insured can fix, such as a loading dock or a driver. One or two large losses may be outliers or a sign of exposure the price doesn't reflect. Severity matters more in liability lines than it used to. A Casualty Actuarial Society and Triple-I analysis estimates that legal system abuse and related litigation trends added[$231.6 billion to $281.2 billion](https://www.casact.org/article/new-cas-and-triple-i-analysis-quantifies-impact-legal-system-abuse-liability-insurance) to US liability insurance losses over the decade to year-end 2024.


### 4. What is still open?


Open and reopened claims carry reserves that can still rise. Look closely at the reserves on recent open claims, since those figures are the carrier's current estimate and will change. A loss run also leaves out claims the carrier doesn't know about yet: incurred losses ordinarily exclude incurred but not reported (IBNR) losses. Big "I" guidance suggests asking the insured whether any claims are[pending but not yet on the loss run](https://www.independentagent.com/vu_resource/preparing-a-winning-underwriting-submission/) .


### 5. How does it compare to premium?


The[NAIC defines loss ratio](https://content.naic.org/glossary-insurance-terms) as incurred losses as a percentage of earned premium. Many loss runs don't show premium, so pull it from the policy or the carrier and calculate the ratio by policy year. For workers' compensation, also compare the loss run with the experience modification factor.[NCCI](https://www.ncci.com/articles/documents/uw_abc_exp_rating.pdf) builds the mod from unit statistical reports, usually covering the latest three years, so the two documents draw on the same claims and should tell the same story.


## **Why loss runs are hard to read at scale**


Loss runs come from hundreds of different sources, and no two look alike. When FurtherAI's engineers[built loss run extraction](https://www.furtherai.com/engineering-blogs/hardest-document-extraction-problem-in-insurance) , they found documents from one page to more than 200, with around 30 fields to capture per claim. In one file, the policy number appeared once as a section header and applied to about 100 claims below it. Blank cells meant "same as the row above." Summary rows looked exactly like claim rows, and in one document they inflated the claim count by 15%.


Most of that work still lands on people. Underwriters in commercial and personal lines spend 41% to 43% of their time on administrative activities, according to[Capgemini](https://www.capgemini.com/insights/research-library/unleashing-growth-the-evolving-role-of-underwriters/) . Accenture's 2025 underwriting research found that only 9% of the underwriting executives surveyed say their organizations use[intelligent ingestion to extract submission data](https://www.accenture.com/en/insights/insurance/underwriting-rewritten) to a large extent today, and 68% expect to within three years. Loss runs are a good example of why: as our guide to[mixed-format submissions](https://www.furtherai.com/blog/mixed-format-submissions-underwriters-strategies) explains, scanned loss runs are among the worst offenders because they aren't machine-readable.


## **How to automate loss run extraction**


Automating loss runs means turning each report, whatever its layout, into the same structured claims table, then checking it before anyone relies on it. Most teams follow five steps.


‍


Step What Happens What It Fixes


1. Collect and classify Loss runs are pulled from email, portals, and submission packets and separated from ACORD forms, SOVs, and other attachments Files that sit unread in an inbox


2. Extract to one schema Every claim row is mapped to the same set of fields, whatever the carrier's layout Rekeying, and claims lost across multi-page tables


3. Normalize Dates, status codes, line names, and net or gross treatment are standardized across carriers Five carriers' conventions in one account


4. Validate Extracted rows are checked against the document's own totals, and gaps are re-read Missed claims, double-counted totals rows, and math errors


5. Summarize and route Frequency, severity, open claims, and large losses are summarized for a person to review Hours spent building the same summary by hand


‍


The validation step decides whether automation can be trusted. In FurtherAI's testing on difficult real-world loss runs, giving the extraction agent a tool to check its output against each document's own totals raised[row count accuracy from 80% to 95%](https://www.furtherai.com/engineering-blogs/hardest-document-extraction-problem-in-insurance) . The gain came from catching missed claims and misread totals rows, which a simple extraction pass returns without any warning.


Normalization matters most when one account has several carriers or administrators. Our guide to[consolidating TPA loss runs](https://www.furtherai.com/blog/mga-claims-data-aggregation) covers the schema side, and for property accounts, loss run data still has to be reconciled with the SOV and inspection reports, as our guide to[multi-source risk data](https://www.furtherai.com/blog/risk-engineer-multi-source-risk-data) explains. Loss runs usually arrive alongside ACORD applications, so the same pipeline often handles[ACORD form data extraction](https://www.furtherai.com/blog/best-ai-acord-form-data-extraction) too.

## **Frequently asked questions**


#### What is a loss run report?


A loss run report is a claims history that an insurance carrier produces for a policyholder. It lists each claim on a policy over a period, with the date of loss, a description, the claim status, and the amounts paid and still reserved. Underwriters use it to judge how an account has performed, and brokers request it when they market or renew coverage.


#### What does incurred mean on a loss run?


Incurred is the total cost of a claim as the carrier sees it on the valuation date: what it has already paid plus what it still has in reserve. A closed claim's incurred usually equals its paid amount. An open claim's incurred can rise or fall as the reserve changes. Check whether the carrier includes claim expenses in incurred, because practice varies.


#### What is the valuation date on a loss run?


The valuation date is the date the carrier froze the figures on the report. Paid amounts and reserves are only accurate as of that day, and open claims keep developing afterwards. Underwriters typically ask for currently valued runs, because a run valued a year ago can understate an account's losses if large claims were still open.


#### How many years of loss runs do underwriters need?


Underwriters commonly ask for three to five years of currently valued loss runs, and Big "I" guidance on submissions recommends five. There is no single industry rule. State laws that require carriers to supply loss runs set different look-back periods, from three policy years in Illinois to five years in Florida, so confirm what each market expects.


#### How long does a carrier have to send loss runs?


It depends on the state. Florida requires carriers to provide loss runs within 15 calendar days of a written request, New York within 10 days, and Illinois within 30 days. Not every state sets a deadline, so check the rules where the policy was written. Brokers who request loss runs early in the renewal cycle avoid waiting on carriers when the marketing window is already short.


#### Can AI read loss runs accurately?


AI can extract loss runs accurately when it checks its own output. FurtherAI's engineering team found that validating extracted rows against each document's own totals raised row count accuracy from 80% to 95% on difficult loss runs. Simple text extraction tends to miss claims or count totals rows as claims, so look for validation and a human review step.
